newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore non-oil exports fall in December.
newsitem.headline: Singapore non-oil exports fall in December.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports in December fell 0.5 percent year-on-year in nominal terms to S$7.46 billion, the Trade Development Board (TDB) said on Monday.
This brought total non-oil domestic export growth for 1996 to 2.7 percent, down sharply from 1995's 13.7 percent.
Total trade growth for 1996 was 5.1 percent but growth this year was expected to be stronger, Chan Kam Fai, director of TDB's trade policy division, told a news conference.
Singapore's total trade is expected to grow between five and seven percent in 1997.
Chan said growth was "probably closer to the upper end of the projected range".
Higher world trade growth and an expected recovery in the global electronics demand by the second half of 1997 were factors seen contributing to the better outlook, he said.
Chan also said the unfavourable factors affecting trade this year would be the lower growth rates expected in three of Singapore's major trading partners.
They are the United States, Japan and Malaysia.
Electronics and related products account for about 70 percent of Singapore's non-oil domestic exports.
Chan said the slower trade growth in 1996 as compared to the 13.2 percent expansion in 1995 was due mainly to the cyclical slowdown in global demand for electronics and related products.
"I would like to stress the slowdown is cyclical, not structural," said Chan.
He noted that between 1992 and 1995, trade growth was at an average of 15.9 percent a year, much higher than "the long term sustainable growth rate of 8-9 percent".
The slowdown in exports led to a slight increase in the trade deficit to S$8.9 billion for 1996 against S$8.8 billion in 1995.
The decline in December non-oil exports confounded economists.
A Reuters poll of 15 financial institutions last week predicted a year-on-year rise of 2.9 percent in December in the non-oil export data.
"The numbers are definitely not as good as expected," said Andy Tan, economist at MMS/Standard & Poor's in Singapore.
"But it is still an improvement from the slump in exports in November. The reason for this must be that the recovery in the electronics sector is patchy," he said.
Reviewing the performance for the year, the TDB said slower growth in 1996 was mainly due to a cyclical slowdown in global demand for electronics and related products.
All major trade components -- except oil -- chalked up lower growth rates.
-- Singapore newsroom (65 8703080)
